procedural_history.originating_court: R/ Civil Special Application No. 16484 of 2022 (Likely a High Court, given the nature of the application)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 26th February, 2024 passed in R/ Civil Special Application No. 16484 of 2022
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court reduced the compensation amount. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in doing so, stating that an appellate court should not substitute its view for that of the lower court unless the decision is perverse, illegal, or otherwise compromised.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants, represented by Ms. Srishti Choudhary, Ms. Shefali Choudhary, and Ms. Namita Choudhary, approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court issued notice on 17th October, 2023. The matter was referred to Lok Adalat but could not be settled. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, implying that it overturned the High Court's reduction of compensation.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court can substitute its own view for that of the court below or interfere with an order simply because another view is possible.

facts: The case involved an appeal against a High Court order.
The High Court had reduced a compensation award previously granted by a lower court.
law: The general rule for appellate courts is that they should not substitute their own view for that of the court below.
An appellate court should not interfere with a lower court's order simply because another view is possible.
Interference by an appellate court is only justified if the lower court's decision is perverse, illegal, or suffers from a similarly serious flaw.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had violated the established principles of appellate review.
It determined that the High Court had interfered with the lower court's order merely because it held a different opinion on the matter, which is not a permissible ground for intervention.
By reducing the compensation, the High Court improperly substituted its own judgment for that of the original court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an appellate court cannot substitute its own view or interfere with a lower court's order just because another view is possible. It held that the High Court erred in doing so and, as a result, allowed the appeals, overturning the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in reducing the compensation awarded by the lower court.

facts: The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) awarded compensation of Rs. 19,35,400 with 7.5% interest to the claimants for the death of the victim in a motor accident.
The High Court, in an appeal, reduced this compensation to Rs. 9,22,336 with 6% interest.
The High Court based its reduction on using the minimum wage rate to calculate the victim's income and a multiplier of 13, determining the victim's age to be 47 based on his Aadhar card.

The claimants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing the victim's age was 45 (as per his School Leaving Certificate), which would mean a multiplier of 14, and they contested the High Court's calculation of the victim's monthly income.
law: An appellate court should not substitute its own view for that of the court below simply because it prefers a different approach.
An appellate court should only interfere with a lower court's decision if it is afflicted by perversity, illegality, or a similar fundamental flaw.
Compensation awarded in motor accident claims must be just and reasonable.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's role was not to decide which method for calculating the victim's income was 'better' (minimum wage vs. rates notified by the District Commissioner).

Since there was no evidence to show that the rates used by the Tribunal were inapplicable, and there was testimony that the deceased was an agriculturist owning a tractor and a JCB, the Supreme Court found no reason for the High Court to interfere with the Tribunal's finding on income.
The Supreme Court also noted that the High Court gave no reason for reducing the interest rate from 7.5% to 6%.

Applying the principle that compensation must be just and reasonable, the Supreme Court found it appropriate to not only reverse the High Court's reduction but to enhance the interest rate to 8% from the date the claim was filed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in reducing the compensation. It held that the High Court should not have substituted its own view for the Tribunal's without finding a clear perversity or illegality. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and recalculated the compensation, awarding a final amount of Rs. 15,00,000 with 8% interest.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate court can substitute its own view for that of the court below or interfere with an order simply because another view is possible.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position, supported by the court, is that an appellate court should not substitute its view for that of the court below merely because another view is possible. Interference is only justified if the lower court's decision is afflicted by perversity, illegality, or a similar vice.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, by defending the High Court's action, implies that the High Court was justified in substituting its view, suggesting the lower court's decision was flawed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in reducing the compensation awarded by the lower court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in reducing the compensation.
The lower court (MACT) correctly determined the age of the deceased based on the School Leaving Certificate.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct to reduce the compensation, implying that the lower court's determination of age was incorrect.

cases.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi
cases.principle: The general rule in appellate proceedings is that a Court sitting in appeal is not to substitute its view for that of the Court below. It is only to see that the decision arrived at is not afflicted by perversity, illegality or any other such vice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court is not to substitute its view for that of the court below or interfere simply because another view is possible. The appellate court's role is to determine if the lower court's decision is afflicted by perversity, illegality, or any other such vice.
obiter: Views aligning with the one referred to above have been taken by the High Court of Judicature of Allahabad in Parvati Kumari v. State of U.P.; the Himachal Pradesh High Court in Kumit Kumar v. State of H.P. and the High Court of Kerala in Sofikul Islam v. State of Kerala.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in reducing the compensation because it improperly substituted its own view for that of the court below. The High Court's interference was unjustified as the lower court's decision was not "afflicted by perversity, illegality or any other such vice," and its determination of the deceased's age based on the School Leaving Certificate was not erroneous.
legal_tests_applied: The general rule insofar as appellate proceedings are concerned is that a Court sitting in appeal is not to substitute its view for that of the Court below.
An appellate court is only to see that the decision arrived at is not afflicted by perversity, illegality or any other such vice which may compromise it beyond redemption.
An order is not to be interfered with simply because another view is possible.
policy_considerations: The final awarded amount was rounded off "in the interest of just compensation".
